title: Hypothermia: signs to look for
asks: what are the signs of hypothermia
how do I know if someone has hypothermia
he stopped shivering is that bad
shivering and slurring his words in the cold
buddy is cold confused and stumbling
can you get hypothermia when its above freezing
cold wet and acting weird whats wrong
partner mumbling and stumbling, very cold, is it hypothermia, over
answer: Early signs: feeling cold, shivering, and withdrawing from other people.
Shivering alone is not hypothermia, but never ignore it: it is a warning sign that the body is getting too cold.
The "umbles": grumbles, mumbles, fumbles and stumbles.
Other signs: confusion, sleepiness, slurred speech, shallow breathing, weak pulse, stiff arms or legs, poor control of body movements, slow reactions, and a change in behavior or appearance.
Shivering may decrease or stop as the person gets colder.

Treat it as severe hypothermia when a very cold person is not shivering and shows mental changes (drowsiness, confusion or unconsciousness) and poor coordination (trouble walking, using the hands or talking).
Severe hypothermia: shivering may stop completely; confusion and disorientation; loss of consciousness; very cold, pale or bluish skin; slow or irregular breathing; weak or absent pulse.
It does not have to be freezing. Hypothermia can happen in mild temperatures if a person is wet.
In a very cold person, breathing can be as slow as 3-4 breaths per minute and the pulse as slow as 10-15 beats per minute. Look for breathing and a pulse for at least 1 minute.
warnings: Hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation.
A person who is hypothermic and not shivering must be evacuated immediately.
The elderly and people who are intoxicated may not show the signs reliably.
No one should be pronounced dead until they have been rewarmed.

quotes.text: Early signs typically include feeling cold, shivering, and withdrawal from social interaction. Clinically, this will first appear as a change in neurological functions. Onset of hypothermia is typically associated with the so-called “umbles”, that is, grumbles, mumbles, fumbles, and stumbles, mirroring how cold affects the body’s muscles and nerves. Symptoms of hypothermia consist of confusion, sleepiness, slurred speech, shallow breathing, weak pulse, low blood pressure, change in behavior or in appearance, shivering or loss of shivering, stiffness in the arms or legs, or poor control over body movements or slow reactions.

As the core body temperature begins to fall, shivering becomes the most noticeable symptom. Shivering alone is not a sign of hypothermia, but it does indicate that the body is having a problem with the cold.
Never ignore shivering--it is a warning sign that the body is getting too cold.

Intense shivering is one of the first signs of body cooling and requires increased attention from leadership because early intervention can prevent the development of hypothermia. The symptoms become progressively worse as body core temperature falls, and if a Soldier becomes sufficiently cold, shivering may actually decrease or even cease altogether

Some easily recognizable signs of hypothermia are: • Vigorous shivering is typically present. • Shivering may decrease or cease as the core temperature continues to fall. • Conscious, but usually apathetic or lethargic. • Confusion. • Sleepiness. • Slurred speech or mumbling. • Slow breathing and drowsiness. • Weak pulse.

If no low reading thermometer is available, it is wise to consider the patient to be in severe hypothermia if the following signs and symptoms are present: • no shivering in spite of being very cold • mental changes such as drowsiness, confusion or unconsciousness • abnormal coordination, trouble walking or using the hands, and difficulty talking.
Severe Hypothermia: ▪ Shivering may stop completely. ▪ Confusion and disorientation. ▪ Loss of consciousness. ▪ Very cold, pale, or bluish skin. ▪ Slow or irregular breathing. ▪ Weak or absent pulse.
Temperatures below freezing are not required for hypothermia to develop.
It can even happen in mild temperatures if a person is wet, which makes it easier to lose body heat.

Signs of breathing or cardiac activity (and/or respiratory and pulse rate) should be sought for at least 1 minute because respiratory rates may be as low as 3-4 breaths per minute, pulse rates as low as 10-15 beats per minute, and pulse volume low and breaths shallow.
The goals of field management of hypothermia are to rescue, examine, insulate, and rapidly transport. Hypothermia is a true medical emergency and requires evacuation.
Provide warm food or fluid to conscious Soldiers. Soldiers who are hypothermic and not shivering must be immediately evacuated.
There are three stages of hypothermia with differing signs and symptoms in each one. The elderly and those individuals who are intoxicated may not demonstrate symptoms or signs reliably.

Because life signs at these temperatures are almost impossible to obtain, no one should be pronounced dead until he or she has been rewarmed; hence the use of the adage, “nobody is dead until warm and dead”.

conflict: The card gives signs only and no temperatures, because the kit's documents disagree on the numbers: TB MED 508 (2026), TC 21-3 (2025) and ATP 3-50.21 (2018) define hypothermia as a core temperature below 95 F (HHS Ship's Medicine Chest, 2003, starts its mild band at 95 F), while ATP 4-02.11 (2026) says it 'begins when the body's core temperature drops below 97' F. The mild / moderate / severe temperature bands also differ between TB MED 508 (89.6-95, 82.4-89.5, below 82.4 F), TC 21-3 (90-95, 80-89, below 80 F), HHS (90-95, 82-90, below 82 F) and ATP 4-02.11 (93-96, 89-93, below 89 F), and TC 21-3 lists 'uncontrollable shivering' under moderate hypothermia where TB MED 508 lists 'reduced shivering' and HHS says 'shivering stops'. If the owner wants a temperature in this card, the figure must be chosen first. Shivering: TB MED 508 lists shivering among the early signs of hypothermia; TC 21-3 says 'Shivering alone is not a sign of hypothermia'; the card states both (lines 1 and 2). The HHS 'consider severe' list is three bullets in the original; the card reads them as all being present together. FEMA P-2064 (2020) was searched: it only says to watch for signs of hypothermia.

review.notes: Re-review of the revised card (full check). New lines checked: A2 combines TC 21-3 'Shivering alone is not a sign of hypothermia' with HHS 'Never ignore shivering--it is a warning sign that the body is getting too cold' - accurate and shown as both; A6 HHS 'consider the patient to be in severe hypothermia if the following signs and symptoms are present'; W3 HHS elderly/intoxicated. Other lines as confirmed in batch 1 (TB MED 508, ATP 4-02.11). Temperature disagreements (now including HHS bands) correctly listed. No PDF junk. Recommended, not blocking: A6 reads HHS's three bullets as all required together ('not shivering and shows mental changes and poor coordination'); the HHS text is ambiguous, and the 'all three' reading under-calls severe hypothermia. The safer reading is 'any of these in a very cold person'. Not blocking because W2 already sends any hypothermic, non-shivering person out immediately.
